slides.1.title: The Vintage Port Declaration System and Top Vintages
slides.1.html:
Vintage Port is not declared every year. Producers usually decide whether to declare in the second spring after harvest, following review by the IVDP (Douro and Port Wine Institute).

📋 The Declaration Process

  1. 18 months after harvest, brief ageing in oak casks (usually about 2–2.5 years)
  2. The producer submits samples to the IVDP to apply for declaration
  3. Once approved, the wine is bottled and needs 10-20 years of bottle ageing to reach its best

slides.2.title: Vertical Tasting: How to Read Ageing Changes
slides.2.html:
🎨 Colour Evolution (Visual Assessment)

Ageing stageColourRim colour
0–5 yearsDeep purple-blackRuby-purple
10–15 yearsDeep rubyBrick red
20–30 yearsGarnetBrown-orange rim
40+ yearsDeep brown-amberPronounced orange-brown

👃 Aroma Evolution

  • Young (0–10 years): blackberry, blueberry, blackcurrant, violet, with noticeable alcohol
  • Middle-aged (15–25 years): dried fruit (fig, date), cedar, tobacco, liquorice, with fruit fading
  • Mature (30+ years): truffle, coffee, chocolate, leather, refined floral notes, with complexity at its peak

📝 Vertical Tasting Note Format

Appearance → Aroma (primary/secondary/tertiary) → Palate (sweetness/acidity/tannin/body) → Finish → Compare against the vintage rating
slides.3.question: How many years of bottle ageing does Vintage Port usually need to reach its best drinking condition?
slides.3.options.3: Like Tawny, cask ageing is enough
slides.3.explanation: Vintage Port spends only about 2–2.5 years in cask before bottling and then needs long-term ageing in bottle. Most top Vintage Ports need 15–25 years before they show complexity, and the greatest vintages can keep evolving for 50–80 years.
